name: Savings Account
tagline: Safe and accessible, earns a little
explanation: Your money sits in a bank account and earns a small interest rate. It is the safest place to keep money you might need soon, like an emergency fund. The trade-off is that returns barely beat inflation.

name: Fixed Deposit (FD)
tagline: Lock in a fixed rate for a set period
explanation: You deposit a lump sum with a bank for a fixed period at a guaranteed rate. FDs are very safe and predictable, but your money is locked until maturity. Good for money you will not need for a year or more.

name: Mutual Funds (SIP)
explanation: A mutual fund pools money from many investors and a fund manager invests it across stocks and bonds. SIP lets you invest a fixed amount every month automatically. Equity funds have historically averaged roughly 10–12% over long periods — but any single year can be far higher or lower.

name: Direct Stocks
tagline: Own a piece of a company directly
explanation: You buy shares of individual companies listed on NSE or BSE. Some picks do very well; others lose heavily — a single bad stock can wipe out gains. Requires research, a demat account, and the stomach for volatility. Illustrative long-term averages are not promises.

name: Gold / SGBs
tagline: A hedge against inflation and uncertainty
explanation: Gold has held value for centuries and tends to rise when stocks fall. Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs) are issued by the RBI and pay 2.5% interest on top of gold price gains. A small gold allocation adds stability to a portfolio.

name: Crypto
explanation: Cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin are extremely volatile and largely unregulated in India. You could make a lot or lose everything. Most financial advisors suggest keeping crypto to less than 5% of your portfolio, if at all.

name: PPF
explanation:
Public Provident Fund (PPF) is a long-term savings scheme backed by the Government of India. Interest is set quarterly — typically around 7–8% — and the full maturity amount is tax-free (exempt-exempt-exempt).

You can open PPF at post offices or banks like SBI and HDFC. Contributions count toward your ₹1.5 lakh 80C limit. Partial withdrawals are allowed from year 7, but the real benefit comes from letting it run the full 15-year cycle.

For safe investors, PPF is often the first long-term pillar alongside EPF — slow, boring, and quietly powerful.

name: Debt Mutual Funds
tagline: Steadier returns from bonds and gilts
explanation:
Debt mutual funds invest in government and corporate bonds instead of stocks. Returns are steadier than equity — typically 6–9% depending on fund type — with lower day-to-day volatility.

Liquid and overnight funds suit emergency money. Short-duration and corporate bond funds suit 1–3 year goals. For higher tax slabs, indexation on long-term gains can beat FD post-tax returns.

Not zero risk — credit and interest-rate moves can cause temporary dips — but far calmer than Nifty swings.

name: Term Insurance
explanation:
Term insurance pays your nominees a lump sum if you die during the policy term — nothing comes back if you survive. That is the point: maximum cover for minimum premium.

A ₹1 crore term plan for a healthy 30-year-old might cost ₹10,000–15,000 per year — cheap compared to ULIPs or endowment plans that mix insurance with investment poorly.

Buy term before you scale investments. If people depend on your income, this is non-negotiable — not a wealth builder, but a safety net.

name: NPS
tagline: Long-term retirement with extra tax benefit
explanation:
National Pension System (NPS) is a retirement account regulated by PFRDA. You choose an mix of equity and debt; returns have historically averaged around 9–11% in active equity tiers over long periods.

Beyond regular 80C, you get an additional ₹50,000 deduction under 80CCD(1B) — useful if you have exhausted PPF and ELSS limits.

Money is locked until age 60 with partial withdrawal rules. Best for disciplined retirement saving, not money you might need in five years.
